promptText: A team grows a consensus ensemble from 3 nodes to 4 nodes, expecting better fault tolerance. What actually happens?
options: Fault tolerance stays at 1 node failure, since majority quorum is floor(N/2)+1 for both sizes (2 of 3, or 3 of 4), while the 4-node cluster now requires one more node to acknowledge every write for no added benefit
Fault tolerance doubles to 2 simultaneous failures because there is one additional node in the ensemble
The ensemble switches from a CP system to an AP system once it has an even number of nodes
Write throughput increases because a 4-node ensemble can serve more concurrent client reads
explanation: Majority quorum is floor(N/2)+1, which is 2 for N=3 and 3 for N=4 — both tolerate exactly 1 failure before losing majority. The fourth node adds replication cost and one more required write-acknowledgment without buying any additional tolerated failure, which is why production ensembles jump straight from 3 to 5, never stopping at 4.

promptText: What does the FLP impossibility result actually prove about consensus in a fully asynchronous network, and what does it NOT prove?
options: It proves no deterministic algorithm can guarantee termination in finite time if even one node can fail; it does not prove consensus is unachievable in practice, since real algorithms relax the termination (liveness) guarantee rather than ever violating agreement (safety)
It proves consensus is theoretically impossible in any network, which is why systems like ZooKeeper and etcd are considered unreliable in production
It proves that safety can never be guaranteed unconditionally, only liveness can be guaranteed unconditionally
It proves that any algorithm relying on a majority quorum is inherently vulnerable to split-brain during a partition
explanation: FLP is a negative result about guaranteed termination under full asynchrony with even one faulty node — it says nothing against agreement ever being violated. Every practical algorithm (Paxos, Raft) responds by guaranteeing safety unconditionally and liveness only once the network behaves reasonably (partial synchrony), which is exactly the relaxation FLP's proof leaves room for.

promptText: A monitoring service in a Paxos deployment only needs to find out the final agreed-upon value and never participates in voting. Which role does it play, and why isn't it simply made an Acceptor too?
options: It's a Learner; making it an Acceptor instead would unnecessarily enlarge the quorum required for every decision, since Acceptors exist to be the smallest group whose majority vote is authoritative
It's a Proposer, since any node that can observe decided state must also be able to propose new values
It's an Acceptor, because every node that wants visibility into the outcome must also cast a vote in Paxos
Paxos only defines two roles, so this node cannot be formally categorized
explanation: Paxos defines Proposer, Acceptor, and Learner precisely so an interested observer doesn't have to join the voting group. Learners find out the decided value without participating in voting, while Acceptors are kept as a minimal, authoritative set — adding unnecessary Acceptors would only make every future majority larger and slower to assemble without adding correctness.

promptText: During a network partition, a 5-node Raft cluster splits into a minority of 2 nodes and a majority of 3 nodes. Why can the minority side never elect its own leader and keep accepting writes at the same time the majority side is operating?
options: 2 votes cannot form a majority of 5, and any two majorities drawn from the same cluster are mathematically guaranteed to share at least one common node, so two disjoint, conflicting majorities can never exist simultaneously
A background watchdog process built into Raft automatically shuts down any ensemble segment smaller than the other
The minority side is technically permitted to elect a leader, but client libraries are hard-coded to reject connections to it
Raft actually requires unanimous agreement from all nodes, not a majority, so any partition at all halts both sides equally
explanation: The quorum-overlap arithmetic (Q + Q > N) guarantees any two majorities of the same cluster share at least one node, making two simultaneous, conflicting leaders mathematically impossible rather than merely unlikely. With only 2 of 5 votes, the minority side structurally cannot assemble a majority and correctly becomes unavailable while the 3-node majority side continues operating.

promptText: A Raft follower stops receiving heartbeats and transitions to Candidate state. What specifically triggers this transition, and what must happen next for it to actually become Leader?
options: Its own randomized election timeout elapses with no heartbeat from a current leader; it must then receive votes from a majority of the cluster in that term before becoming Leader
It receives an explicit StepDown message from the previous leader instructing it to take over as the new leader
It notices its log has fewer entries than a peer's log and automatically promotes itself to catch the cluster up
Receiving a single vote from any other node is sufficient, since Raft does not require majority support to become leader
explanation: A follower assumes the leader is gone only once its own randomized election timeout elapses with no heartbeat, at which point it increments its term, votes for itself, and requests votes from peers. It only becomes Leader for that term after collecting votes from a majority of the cluster — seeing it campaign does not mean it has already won.

promptText: Why is etcd a poor fit as the primary datastore for a high-throughput, frequently-updated application dataset, even though it is strongly consistent?
options: Every write must be replicated to and acknowledged by a majority of nodes before being committed, which bounds throughput well below a purpose-built datastore; etcd is architected for comparatively low-volume coordination data, not high-volume primary storage
etcd has a hard architectural limit of only a few hundred total keys it can ever store
etcd only supports eventually consistent reads, making it unsuitable for any workload that needs correctness guarantees
etcd requires every write to execute a full Basic Paxos two-phase protocol, which ZooKeeper's ZAB protocol does not need
explanation: Consensus-backed stores pay a full majority round-trip on every write, which is fine for the comparatively low-volume coordination data (locks, leader identity, configuration) they're designed for, but becomes a throughput and latency wall for high-volume application data — this is a design-fit mismatch, not something tuning can fix.

promptText: In Basic Paxos's Phase 2, a proposer collects promises from a majority of acceptors, and one acceptor reports it had already accepted a value under an earlier, lower proposal number. What must the proposer do, and why?
options: Send its Accept request carrying that already-accepted value instead of its own, because overriding it with a different value could let two different values both end up decided across overlapping quorums, which would violate safety
Discard the current round entirely and restart Phase 1 from scratch with a brand-new, unrelated value
Send its own original value regardless, since Phase 1's only purpose is to collect acceptor votes, not to discover prior values
Immediately abort, since any already-accepted value found during Phase 1 means consensus has become impossible for this round
explanation: Reusing the highest-numbered already-accepted value reported in Phase 1 — rather than overriding it with the proposer's own value — is the single detail that makes Paxos safe, since it prevents a second proposer from causing two different values to each be accepted by a majority.

promptText: Why can a Raft leader mark a log entry committed and respond success to the client as soon as only a majority of followers have acknowledged it, rather than waiting for every follower?
options: Any future majority needed for a leader election or further commit is guaranteed to overlap with the majority that already stored this entry, so the entry can never be lost or contradicted later; waiting for every node would only add latency without adding safety
Followers that haven't yet acknowledged the entry are automatically considered failed and permanently removed from the cluster
Raft only provides eventual consistency, so the entry isn't actually durable until every single node has applied it to its state machine
The leader cannot reliably detect which followers are alive, so a majority is used purely as a timeout heuristic rather than a safety mechanism
explanation: The same majority-quorum overlap that prevents split-brain also guarantees a committed entry survives any future leader change, since any subsequent majority must share at least one node that already has it. Requiring all nodes to acknowledge would block progress on a single slow or unreachable follower with no additional durability benefit.

promptText: Why does a Raft node refuse to vote for a candidate whose log is less up-to-date than its own, and what would break without that check?
options: Without it, a node with a stale, incomplete log could win an election and, through Raft's log-repair process, overwrite followers' logs and silently discard entries that had already been committed and acknowledged to clients
Without it, split votes would become permanent, and the cluster would never be able to elect any leader at all
The check exists purely to speed up elections; omitting it would only slow down leader election, not threaten correctness
It prevents a single node from being allowed to become a candidate more than once within the same term
explanation: Since a committed entry already exists on a majority of nodes, requiring a candidate's log to be at least as up-to-date as any voter's guarantees that any candidate who wins a majority already holds every committed entry — closing off the data-loss scenario where a stale new leader erases previously-committed, client-acknowledged work.

promptText: A process holding a Curator InterProcessMutex pauses for a GC cycle longer than the ZooKeeper session timeout, and ZooKeeper reassigns the lock to the next waiter. What risk does this create, and what mitigates it?
options: The original process may resume unaware it lost the lock and keep executing its critical section concurrently with the new holder; a fencing token — a monotonically increasing number checked by the downstream resource — prevents the stale holder's late action from being honored
No risk exists, since ZooKeeper forcibly terminates the original process's JVM the instant its session expires
This risk is unique to Paxos-based systems and does not apply to Raft-based coordination services like etcd
Setting the session timeout to zero eliminates the risk completely with no other operational trade-off
explanation: ZooKeeper's guarantee is only that it never believes two clients hold the lock at once — it cannot stop a resumed, unaware process from still acting as if it holds the lock. A fencing token checked by the actual resource being modified closes that gap by rejecting a stale holder's late action, regardless of what the holder itself believes.

promptText: A team configures every Raft node with an identical, fixed election timeout. After the cluster's first leader failure, elections repeatedly fail to produce a winner across several terms. What is the cause, and what fixes it?
options: All followers time out at the same instant and split the vote identically term after term; randomizing each node's timeout makes one follower reliably time out first and collect a majority before competitors even start campaigning
A fixed timeout causes a permanent network partition to form between the followers themselves
The cause is unrelated to the timeout setting and instead indicates the cluster was sized with an even number of nodes
A fixed timeout prevents followers from ever detecting that the leader has failed, so no election is ever triggered at all
explanation: Identical fixed timeouts mean every follower becomes a candidate at the same moment, splitting the vote repeatedly with no majority winner. Randomization is the specific mechanism that makes split votes rare and self-resolving, by making it highly likely exactly one follower starts its election before any other candidate appears.

promptText: Why is ZooKeeper's ZAB protocol described as more specialized than general Paxos, rather than simply being a reimplementation of it?
options: ZAB is optimized specifically for a single leader broadcasting a strictly ordered sequence of state updates to followers, which is a narrower problem than Basic Paxos's more general, symmetric any-node-can-propose model
ZAB eliminates the need for majority quorums entirely by relying on a fixed, pre-assigned leader that is never re-elected
ZAB is specialized because it tolerates only Byzantine failures, whereas Paxos tolerates only simple crash failures
ZAB is a strict subset of Paxos that removes the Accept phase from the protocol entirely
explanation: ZAB's narrower, leader-broadcast workload let its designers build something simpler and more directly usable for ZooKeeper's actual replication pattern than general Paxos, which must also handle the fully symmetric, multi-proposer case ZooKeeper never actually needs.

promptText: A 5-node Raft ensemble is deployed with a 2-2-1 split across three regions (A, B, C). Compare what happens if Region A (2 nodes) is fully isolated versus a different deployment where one region holds 3 of the 5 nodes and that region is isolated instead.
options: With the 2-2-1 split, losing Region A still leaves 3 of 5 nodes (B's 2 plus C's 1) forming a majority, so the cluster keeps operating; but if one region instead holds 3 of 5 nodes and that region is isolated, the remaining 2 nodes cannot form a majority and the whole cluster stalls even though two entire regions survived
Node-to-region distribution never actually matters for availability — only the total node count across all regions determines whether the cluster keeps running
Losing any single region always halts the entire cluster, regardless of how the nodes happen to be distributed across regions
Concentrating 3 of 5 nodes in one region is always the safer design, because it gives that region a strong internal majority on its own
explanation: Majority-quorum math cares only about how many nodes remain reachable, not how many regions remain reachable — a 2-2-1 layout survives losing any one region, while concentrating a majority (3 of 5) in a single region turns that region's isolation into a full outage even though the other regions are healthy, which is exactly why node-to-region placement is a deliberate design decision, not an afterthought.

promptText: You are migrating leader election from a hand-rolled database-lock mechanism to a Raft-based coordination service, and must guarantee there is never a window where both mechanisms are simultaneously treated as authoritative. Which migration approach achieves this safely?
options: Run both in parallel with the database lock as sole authority while the new service registers in observe-only mode and logs any disagreement; only after sustained agreement across real leader-change events, including an actual failure, flip a single feature flag making the new service authoritative, keeping the old lock briefly as a fallback alarm before removing it
Switch every instance to the new coordination service atomically in one deployment with no observation period, since Raft's correctness guarantees make a transition window unnecessary
Run both mechanisms as co-equal, independently authoritative sources of truth at the same time, accepting that disagreements will be rare enough not to matter
Disable leader election entirely during the migration window and allow every instance to act as leader until the cutover finishes
explanation: The key invariant is that exactly one mechanism is authoritative at every point in time; observe-only parallel running validates the new system against real failure events without ever letting two sources simultaneously decide leadership, and a single flag flip performs the actual cutover atomically rather than gradually or ambiguously.

promptText: Consensus can guarantee "exactly one leader at a time," but distributed systems generally cannot guarantee "exactly-once message delivery" across an unreliable network. Why does one guarantee hold while the structurally similar-sounding one does not?
options: Exactly-once leadership is an internal agreement among nodes that coordinate directly via majority voting, making two conflicting majorities mathematically impossible; exactly-once delivery depends on a sender being unable to distinguish "the message was lost" from "the acknowledgment was lost" over an unreliable link, an ambiguity no amount of receiver-side agreement can resolve
Both guarantees are actually equally achievable; exactly-once delivery is a myth from outdated tutorials, since modern Raft-based systems already provide it natively
Exactly-once leadership isn't truly guaranteed either — it only appears reliable because split-brain incidents are rarely reported publicly
The two are really the same guarantee under different names, and Raft uses an identical mechanism to solve both problems simultaneously
explanation: Quorum overlap resolves leadership because all the relevant parties (the cluster's own nodes) can directly vote and observe each other's votes. Message delivery across a network involves no such mutual voting — the sender fundamentally cannot tell a lost message apart from a lost acknowledgment, which is why systems settle for at-least-once delivery combined with idempotency instead of trying to guarantee exactly-once.
